summary: This is a careful reading of Anthropic's terms, not legal advice. Anthropic's Claude Code legal page (modified 5 Oct 2026) covers this case directly. A product may run Claude Code if the binary is unmodified, no built-in sign-in method is removed or restricted, the product never pays for, resells or intermediates Claude usage, and each end user signs in with their own credentials. The page also says its credential rules do not stop an end user signing in to the unmodified binary with their own subscription, even where a platform hosts Claude Code. A Vector chat view driven by claude -p is therefore in a grey zone, and Vector's own prompt framing makes it worse (see conditions). The likelier real-world risks are Anthropic billing this use as extra usage, or a technical change (bare mode becoming the -p default), rather than a clear breach.

Rename the entry 'Cursor CLI' (or just 'Cursor'), in line with Cursor's docs and its naming rule.
Show no Cursor brand colours or visual styling elsewhere in the integration, and imply no partnership.
Add an explicit not-affiliated line, beyond the current 'Names and logos belong to their owners'.
summary: Using the name 'Cursor' in text is fine under nominative fair use. Cursor's brand page asks only that it be called 'Cursor', not 'Cursor AI' or 'Cursor Code', and offers downloadable logos, including the cube on its own. It states no licence and no rules for third parties. Cursor's Terms (updated 3 Sep 2026) disclaim implied licences, although that clause is about the Service. Showing Cursor's logo therefore rests on fair use alone, and US nominative fair use favours the bare name: in Tabari the court said the dealer could make its point without Lexus's 'visual trappings', and that those cues could suggest affiliation. Showing only Cursor's and Kilo's logos while every other agent gets letters also makes Cursor stand out in the list, which slightly raises the risk that it looks like a relationship. Vector's label 'Cursor Agent' also does not match Cursor's docs, which call the product 'Cursor CLI'.

conditions: Show no Invertocat, Octocat, Copilot icon or 'GitHub Copilot' lockup.

summary: GitHub's brand page allows a permitted GitHub logo to tell people that a project integrates with GitHub, as long as it is less prominent than your own brand, unaltered, and doesn't suggest you are GitHub or that GitHub endorses you. For everything else it requires prior written permission, and its legal note claims no use of any kind is allowed without it. That claim goes further than trademark law, but GitHub's Terms (effective 27 Apr 2026, s.G.2) make the guidelines binding on anyone who uses GitHub's marks, and Vector almost certainly has GitHub accounts. Since 2025 Copilot has no standalone logo for anyone to use. Microsoft's guidelines, which matter because Copilot is also a Microsoft mark, expressly allow truthful, unaltered, less prominent references in text, and forbid Microsoft logos and icons without a licence. A plain-text name with a neutral 'CP' badge fits both GitHub's integration allowance and Microsoft's rules.

label: research:trademarks
conditions: Show no Google 'G', Gemini spark or Antigravity marks unless approved through Google's Brand Permissions process.

Imply no relationship with Google or endorsement by it, and add a not-affiliated line.

summary: Google's brand guidance lets anyone refer to Google or its products in plain text in an informational context without asking, provided they follow its trademark rules. Logos and other 'Brand Features' need Google's approval, and any approved use must carry a trademark notice. The proper-usage rules say: no display that implies a relationship with Google, never fold Google marks into your own product names, set the mark apart from surrounding text, and spell it exactly as on Google's Trademark List. Google's Terms (effective 30 Jul 2026) send anyone wanting to use its branding or logos to Brand Permissions. Gemini CLI is Apache-2.0, which grants no trademark rights, and the Antigravity terms have no brand clause. Plain-text names with letter badges fit Google's 'go for it' category, but the examples Google gives are books, articles and websites, not a commercial app's interface.

label: research:trademarks
conditions: Show no Meta or Muse logo unless approved through Meta's Brand Review process.

Imply no partnership, sponsorship or endorsement, and add a not-affiliated line.
Keep the Contributor-mode data note accurate and sourced. It is factual, not branding, but inaccuracy would undercut fair use.
summary: Meta's brand page says its trademarks may be used only as its guidelines provide or with Meta's permission. Every use of the Meta logo needs approval, and Meta marks may never form part of another company, product or domain name. For text, the page says only to follow its guidance, giving examples such as 'Built with Llama', so referring to a Meta product in text is clearly contemplated. Meta's open-source trademark policy expressly allows nominative use of the name only, with no logo and nothing suggesting sponsorship, but it covers only Meta's open-source marks. Listing Muse Code in plain text with a neutral 'MC' badge and no logo fits nominative fair use and Meta's stated approach. Vector's own note correctly says a logo would need Meta's approval.

Name the product accurately: the CLI is 'Kilo CLI' (command `kilo`), while 'Kilo Code' is Kilo's name for its VS Code and JetBrains extensions. Use 'Kilo' or 'Kilo CLI'.

Keep the not-affiliated wording in the footnote.
summary: Kilo is the only vendor in this group whose page expressly lets third parties use its logos. Its ecosystem guidelines welcome developers to use any logo from Kilo's open-source repositories to show association or compatibility (as in 'Works with Kilo'), provided it doesn't suggest an official Kilo product. Vector's kilo.svg matches the repository file (black square with a #FAF74F mark), and the code records that permission. The same page sets a '[Your Product Name] for Kilo' naming format, which doesn't apply because Vector doesn't use Kilo in its own name. It also sets maintenance expectations (check compatibility monthly, state supported versions) for community projects using the Kilo name, and Kilo may ask a project to drop the name. The MIT licence covers copyright in the code, not the Kilo marks.

Add an explicit not-affiliated line so the listing cannot reasonably suggest a relationship.
summary: Cline's brand page publishes logos, icons and avatars but sets no rules for third parties. Its Terms (last modified 25 Sep 2025) prohibit users, without prior written consent, from identifying or referring to Cline in a way that could reasonably imply a relationship. They also prohibit any use of Cline's IP that the Terms don't expressly permit. These bind Vector only to the extent Vector or its team are Cline users, and the relationship clause concerns implying a connection, not merely naming. A plain-text 'Cline' entry with a neutral 'CL' badge, plus a clear not-affiliated line, fits nominative fair use and doesn't imply a relationship.

label: research:trademarks

Keep the name lowercase 'goose', as the project writes it, and never in a Vector product name.
Imply no AAIF or Linux Foundation sponsorship or endorsement.
summary: The goose repository says goose is part of the Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation. The Linux Foundation's trademark policy allows fair use of word marks to make true factual statements. It still asks for a trademark notice on the first or most prominent use, and requires written permission before any LF logo appears on websites or marketing. The policy also says a mark must not be part of your product name, must not be more prominent than your own name, and must not imply endorsement. The AAIF brand page adds similar rules for AAIF's own marks, with a sample not-affiliated statement. Vector's plain-text 'goose' with a 'GO' letter badge and no logo fits both, apart from the missing trademark notice.

label: research:trademarks
conditions: Add a JetBrains-specific attribution, for example 'Junie is a trademark of JetBrains s.r.o.', and link to www.jetbrains.com, such as from the docs link or the footnote.
Spell 'Junie' and 'JetBrains' exactly as JetBrains does.
Keep the badge clearly Vector's own. JetBrains forbids imitating its brand assets, and its product icons are traditionally letter-based tiles, so the 'JU' tile should not look like a JetBrains icon.
If Vector ever shows the logo, use JetBrains' downloaded file unaltered, with the product-logo attribution.
Imply no JetBrains approval, endorsement or partnership.
summary: JetBrains has the most explicit permission of any vendor here. Its brand guidelines welcome references to its products, including built-in integrations, with examples like '[Product] works with IntelliJ IDEA'. They grant a limited licence to anyone who follows the guidelines, and Junie appears among the downloadable product logos and icons. In return they ask a lot: every use of JetBrains Brand Assets, which by definition include names and trademarks, should link back to jetbrains.com and carry an attribution clearly marking them as JetBrains' property. Exact spelling is required, and JetBrains marks may not be more prominent than your own, imitated, or used in your own product names. The guidelines say that using JetBrains Brand Assets means accepting them, and they are governed by Czech law. A plain-text 'Junie CLI' row with a 'JU' badge is permitted in substance, but Vector's generic footnote probably falls short of JetBrains' attribution request.

label: research:trademarks
conditions: Show no Kimi or Moonshot logo in Vector without Moonshot's written consent.
Use only the plain-text name 'Kimi Code'. Imply no endorsement or affiliation, and add a not-affiliated line.
Don't use 'Kimi' in any Vector product, feature or plan name.
summary: Moonshot's Kimi logo usage terms license Kimi logos, trademarks and brand assets only for editorial, media and non-commercial promotional use. They forbid altering the logo and forbid implying endorsement or affiliation without written consent. Vector is commercial, so the licence doesn't cover showing a Kimi logo, and Vector correctly shows letters instead. The terms don't separate the name from the logo, so their 'trademarks' wording could be read to reach commercial text references too. For the plain-text name, Vector relies on nominative fair use, not on Moonshot's licence.

vendor: Factory, Amp Frontier Corporation, Alibaba (Qwen), Earendil
label: research:trademarks
conditions: Show no vendor logos unless the vendor gives written permission.
Use exact product names, including the company name where it matters: 'Factory Droid', not 'Droid' alone, since DROID is a mark owned by another company.
Write names in plain text, never more prominent than Vector's own brand, and never in a Vector product, feature, plan or domain name.

Change the footnote from 'Names and logos belong to their owners' to an explicit statement, for example: 'Product names are trademarks of their respective owners; Vector is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by them.'
Keep every factual note (billing, data use, tool behaviour) accurate and sourced. A misleading claim next to a vendor's name undermines fair use.
summary: No brand or trademark-usage page was found for these four vendors. What exists: Factory's terms (updated 15 Oct 2026) say the agreement gives neither party rights to the other's name or logo. Amp's terms say its marks belong to Amp. Qwen Code is Apache-2.0, whose s.6 grants no trademark rights. pi is MIT with no trademark policy. With no permission granted, the only basis is US nominative fair use: the product can't be identified without the name, only the name is used, and nothing suggests sponsorship. Plain-text names, neutral letter badges and no logos fit that test well. The EU and UK reach a similar result through an 'honest practices' test (EU Trade Mark Regulation Art. 14(1)(c) and (2)), which fails if the use suggests a commercial connection or takes unfair advantage of the mark.

agent: Qwen Code with an Alibaba Cloud Coding Plan or Token Plan subscription key (sk-sp- keys, Model Studio or QwenCloud)
label: verify:qwen-jetbrains:Qwen Code with an Alibaba Cloud Coding
conditions: Each headless Qwen turn must come from a prompt the user typed and sent, with one run per send. Never run Qwen from Vectorscope, background or parallel subagents, auto-continue loops, schedules, batch fan-out, or a re-send that Vector starts itself. The CLI's own internal retry on an overloaded error is fine.
Run Qwen only on the user's own machine. QwenCloud Token Plan Personal is meant for a single device per user, so never move a plan-key session to Vector Cloud, a hosted runner or a remote sandbox.

Nobody else may drive a user's Qwen session. Multiplayer, Follow, invite guests and Cloud sharing must not let another person type into it or start runs on it, because the plans are for the subscriber's exclusive use with one key per subscriber or seat.

Never read, log, display, sync or upload the key, including in scrollback, crash reports and shared transcripts. Leave all auth to Qwen Code's own /auth or settings. An exposed key may be disabled automatically.

Keep the CLI unmodified. Do not override its base URL, endpoint, user agent or headers. If Alibaba returns 'Only available for Coding Agents', show the error to the user and point them to the terminal tier rather than working around it.

Offer Qwen in the terminal tier too, with a one-line note that links Alibaba's own pages and says plan keys are for interactive use in coding tools. Do not detect the plan by reading the user's key or settings. Consider driving the chat tier through `qwen --acp`, the editor-integration mode Qwen documents for Zed, which fits 'interactive client' better than a mode Qwen describes as for scripting.
Do not market Vector as a way to use an Alibaba Coding Plan or Token Plan, and do not say Alibaba approves of it.

Do not promise privacy for Qwen runs. Model Studio's Token Plan Personal uses inputs and outputs for service improvement and model optimisation, and QwenCloud Token Plan inference involves cross-border data transfer.

Re-read these pages before launch and on each release. Most of them carry no date, and the plans change often: the weekly quota was removed on 22 Sept 2026, and QwenCloud's Coding Plan pages now redirect to Token Plan.
summary: I think the earlier 'unclear' verdict is a little too harsh, though most of its conditions are right. Alibaba bans using a plan key for automation scripts, custom application backends and non-interactive batch calls; the Chinese Coding Plan text bans that use 'in the form of API calls'. The Token Plan Personal terms say outright that calls a user starts interactively inside a tool are normal use. Qwen Code is a listed tool, and Vector's chat tier runs one unmodified `qwen -p` turn for each prompt the user types, on the user's own device and key, without Vector ever calling the API. Alibaba's own Qwen team docs (updated 22 Oct 2026) go further than Vector does: they recommend Coding Plan auth for headless and CI setups, and they document third-party hosts such as Zed running the CLI programmatically (`qwen --acp`). Some risk remains, because the English Coding Plan page (11 Oct 2026) also bans 'other non-interactive scenarios', Qwen calls -p mode a tool for scripting and automation, and Alibaba enforces automatically with suspensions or key bans that land on Vector's users. So the use looks permitted only while Vector stays a human-driven chat front end.

label: verify:credits:pi: Claude Pro/Max sign-in (rule)
conditions: Never mention, recommend, document, demo, screenshot or market pi as a way to use a Claude Pro or Max subscription. That covers the launcher, onboarding, docs, site, changelog, investor material and support replies.

Never read pi's auth.json. Never copy, refresh or pass Anthropic OAuth tokens. Never run 'pi auth print-bearer-token', 'pi auth print-api-key' or 'pi auth check --credentials'. Never automate pi's /login or pick the 'Anthropic (Claude Pro/Max)' option for the user.

Add Vector's own terms note to the pi card, since pi's own extra-usage warning is interactive-only and does not reach the --mode json chat tier. Suggested wording: 'Anthropic's terms restrict Claude Pro/Max sign-in in third-party tools, and Vector doesn't support it for pi. Connect Anthropic in pi with an API key, or use Claude Code for your Claude subscription.' Keep the sign-in hint neutral ('Type /login inside pi to connect a provider.').

Do not knowingly carry Anthropic subscription traffic in pi's chat tier. Before a chat-tier run, or when pi's event stream shows provider 'anthropic', check with pi's own 'pi auth check --provider anthropic --json --no-refresh' (never with --credentials). It reports only status and authType. If authType is 'oauth', do not start or continue the Anthropic run in Vector's chat view. Show the note and offer an API key, or Claude Code for the subscription.

Drop the ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN variable name from the environment Vector passes to pi in the chat tier, without reading its value. pi treats any sk-ant-oat token as subscription auth and sends Claude Code's identity with it.
Keep pi's model list in Vector empty or neutral. Never surface Claude-subscription models for pi, and never imply that pi gives access to a Claude plan.
Keep Vector's own rule: no Claude.ai login anywhere in Vector. Claude subscription use goes only through the unmodified Claude Code binary, which the legal page expressly allows.
In the terminal tier, Vector should act as a plain terminal and add no shortcut, preset or promotion for this route. pi shows its own extra-usage warning there.

Re-check before each release, and sooner if any of these happen: pi stops sending Claude Code's identity, Anthropic names pi as an approved usage-credits tool, or Anthropic clarifies how it treats launchers of third-party harnesses. Loosen or tighten the conditions to match.
summary: "Risky" was too lenient. The earlier review missed two primary sources. pi's request code (main, updated 23 Oct 2026) drops pi's own client identity when it holds a Claude subscription token and presents itself as Claude Code. It sends a claude-cli user-agent, x-app: cli, Claude Code beta flags, a 'You are Claude Code' system prompt and Claude Code tool names, under a comment that reads 'Stealth mode'. Anthropic's current help article on Claude login prohibits third-party tools that misrepresent their identity to Anthropic's servers or route third-party traffic against subscription limits. The Claude Code legal page also bars third parties from offering Claude.ai login. So pi's 'Anthropic (Claude Pro/Max)' route breaks Anthropic's stated rules, and Vector must not support it, promote it or knowingly carry it in its chat view. Vector's own legal exposure stays low and indirect if it follows the conditions below, because it never touches the credential and is not a party to the user's Consumer Terms. This verdict covers only this route. pi with an API key or another provider is a separate question. There is one more reason to act: pi's own warning that Anthropic bills this usage as extra usage appears only in interactive mode, so users of Vector's headless chat tier never see it. Not legal advice.

label: verify:trademarks:Claude Code
conditions: Have the company accept Anthropic's Commercial Terms, for example by opening a Claude Console organisation in Vector's name. The legal page makes this a condition of running Claude Code in your products.
Launch only the user's own installed, unmodified claude binary, and never bundle or patch a copy.

Never remove or restrict a built-in sign-in method. That rules out forcing --bare, writing forceLoginMethod, stripping or injecting ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, and pointing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at a Vector server.
Never read, store or pass on Claude credentials, keychain entries or setup-token output. Sign-in must finish in Anthropic's own flow.
Never pay for, resell, bundle or intermediate Claude usage. Codium credits must not buy Claude Code runs, and Claude Code must not run on any Vector or Vector Cloud host.
Never let one person's login serve another person. In multiplayer, invite-guest, Follow or shared sessions, a guest must not be able to prompt or resume the host's Claude Code run.

Never use the user's Claude Code login for Vector's own features: Vectorscope, titles, summaries, brain indexing, helper subagents, and scheduled or background jobs. Every run must start from an explicit user action, and Vector should avoid fanning out many parallel runs by default.
Do not change how Claude Code identifies itself to Anthropic. That means no spoofed client headers or entrypoint variables.
Use 'Claude Code' only as plain text that names the user's installed CLI, for example 'runs your installed claude command'. Never put it in the name of a Vector product, feature, plan or mode.
Show no Anthropic or Claude logo, spark, mascot, ASCII art or brand colours, and don't imitate Claude Code's interface. Keep the CC badge neutral; slate is safer than the warm sand tone #c4ad86.
Add a line saying Vector is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Anthropic, because the current footnote does not say this. Never call Anthropic a partner.
Say that Claude Code usage is billed by Anthropic under the user's own plan. Never present it as included in Vector's plans or as free.
Show only model names Anthropic publishes. All twelve entries in CLAUDE_MODELS match its models page as of 23 Oct 2026.
Re-check the terms before each release and keep a remote off-switch. If --bare becomes the default for -p, fall back to the terminal tier and never extract tokens as a workaround.
summary: The first review missed the most relevant document, the Legal and compliance page in the Claude Code docs. It lets a product run Claude Code when three things hold: the binary is unmodified, its sign-in methods are left intact, and each end user signs in with their own subscription or key and is billed by Anthropic directly. The same page says nothing stops an end user signing in to the unmodified binary with their own subscription. It also lets a product say, accurately and in plain text, that it runs Claude Code, as long as the name stays out of the product's own names and logos and nothing implies endorsement. Vector fits these rules, and Anthropic's Help Center (update of 7 Oct 2026) says claude -p and third-party apps still work within subscription limits, so the earlier verdict of 'unclear' is too harsh. Three risks remain: running Claude Code in a product is tied to accepting the Commercial Terms; Anthropic calls claude -p 'the Agent SDK via the CLI', and its SDK branding rule forbids the label 'Claude Code'; and the Usage Policy taking effect on 12 Nov 2026 bans services that route requests through consumer subscriptions or misrepresent the client. This is a reading of the terms, not legal advice.

agent: Cursor Agent (Cursor CLI, binary agent / cursor-agent)
label: verify:trademarks:Cursor (listed in Vector as 'Cursor Agent'
conditions: Only run the official, unmodified Cursor binary, using its documented flags and commands: -p, --output-format stream-json, --model, --resume, --trust, --force, login, status, models. Never call Cursor's private endpoints. Never extract or reuse the user's Cursor tokens. Never route Cursor models into Vector's own agent or proxy. A forum reply that appears to be from Cursor staff says third-party providers that call private endpoints breach ToS section 1.5.

Start every Cursor run from a specific action by the user, on that user's own Cursor account. Vectorscope, background subagents, schedules and other Vector automation must not start Cursor runs unless the user asks. This keeps Vector as far as possible from the AUP's automated-access bullet.

Never resell, share or pool Cursor access. Never let one user's Cursor account serve another user or a guest, including in multiplayer and Follow sessions. ToS section 1.5(iii) forbids renting, leasing or selling the Service, and the AUP forbids reselling Inputs or Suggestions and dodging billing or rate limits.

Never use Cursor's outputs (code, transcripts, events) to train, fine-tune or evaluate Vector's own models, such as Velocity or Codium. ToS section 1.5(v) and the AUP forbid building a competing model from the Service or its Suggestions. Keep Cursor transcripts on the user's machine, or at least out of every training pipeline.

Before the user's first Cursor run, say clearly that --force and --trust let Cursor change files and run commands without asking. Keep those runs in the isolated worktree. Under ToS section 1.7, the user takes on the risk of auto-executed code.

Label Cursor runs as Cursor in Vector's chat view. Cursor's work must not look like Vector's own service, and Vector's service must not look like Anysphere's. The AUP forbids services that appear to come from Anysphere when they do not, and the reverse.

Logo: the safest choice is letters, like the other agents. If the cube stays, use Cursor's own file unaltered, at the same size and treatment as every other badge, always beside the name, and never more prominent than Vector's own brand. Use no Cursor colours or styling anywhere else. Do not use the logo on the landing page, in ads or in store listings without Cursor's written permission. Remove it promptly if Anysphere asks.
Change the footnote to say explicitly that Vector is not affiliated with or endorsed by Anysphere or any of the other vendors, in addition to saying that names and logos belong to their owners.

Naming: 'Cursor Agent' (from Cursor's own launch post) and 'Cursor CLI' (from the current docs) are both acceptable. Never use 'Cursor AI' or 'Cursor Code'. Do not advertise a partnership or a feature like 'Cursor built in'. A plain-text 'works with Cursor CLI' is fine.

Recommended before a paid commercial launch: ask Cursor in writing (support or sales) to confirm two things. First, that a desktop app starting the user's own Cursor CLI in print mode at the user's request is within the 11 Aug 2026 AUP. Second, that showing the cube in a list of compatible agents is acceptable. Keep the reply on file.
summary: My reading of the terms is that Vector's way of running Cursor is allowed, under conditions. Vector runs the user's own unmodified Cursor CLI, signed in to the user's own account, with flags Cursor documents. Cursor's docs say print mode is for 'scripts, CI pipelines, or automation' and that ACP is for 'building custom clients and integrations'. Cursor's own blog promotes running the CLI inside JetBrains IDEs on the user's Cursor account. Forum replies, apparently from Cursor staff, describe resale of Cursor itself as the thing the ToS forbids, not apps that use it. The other researcher was too harsh on the logo and the name, and missed the biggest textual risk. Cursor's AUP (11 Aug 2026), which forms part of the ToS and wins any conflict, bans access 'through automated or non-human means, whether through a bot, script, or otherwise' with no exception. That clashes with Cursor's own headless docs and is most likely aimed at unauthorized bots, but Cursor has not resolved the clash in writing. The logo has no licence and rests on nominative fair use. The risk is modest and mostly a removal request, because Cursor offers the cube as a separate download and Vector shows it unaltered, badge-sized and beside the name. The name 'Cursor Agent' is acceptable: Cursor titled its own launch post 'Cursor Agent CLI', and its brand rule bans only 'Cursor AI' and 'Cursor Code'.
